source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Founding claim: individual differences in ultimate performance are largely explained by accumulated deliberate practice (effortful, goal-directed, with feedback, designed to improve). Not opened this session; claim text quoted from Macnamara 2014 and Hambrick 2020.
numbers: Violin study figures (from memory, unverified here): best violinists about 7,400 hours by age 18, good about 5,300, music-teacher group about 3,400.
quote: individual differences in ultimate performance can largely be accounted for by differential amounts of past and current levels of practice
limits: Original is not about chess. Chess was added by Charness et al. (1996, 2005). Numbers here were not checked this session.
agent_relevance: Defines the construct our agent copies: practice that is designed, goal-set and fed back, not mere repetition.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Games (chiefly chess) had the strongest practice-performance link of any domain, yet practice still left most variance unexplained.
numbers: Games: 11 effect sizes, r = .51, 26% of variance (p<.001). Music 21% (r=.46), sports 18% (r=.42), education 4% (r=.21), professions <1% (r=.05, p=.62). The Games N in Table 1 is garbled in the PDF text, so not recorded.
quote: the claim that individual differences in performance are largely accounted for by differences in deliberate practice is not supported
limits: Mostly retrospective questionnaires. Restricted range among experts. Authors define DP as structured activities designed to improve; Ericsson rejects this definition.
agent_relevance: Even in the best case, about 74% of skill variance is not practice hours. The agent should not assume more rehearsal alone buys skill.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) meta-analysis (moderators)
finding: How practice was measured changed the result: log-based measures gave weak links, retrospective questionnaires gave stronger ones.
numbers: Variance explained by method: 5% log (r=.22), 12% questionnaire (r=.34), 20% interview (r=.45). By predictability: 24% high (r=.49), 12% medium (r=.35), 4% low (r=.21). Solitary-only DP: 11% overall, games 23%. With reliability .80 assumed for both measures: r=.43 overall, games 41%.
limits: Few primary studies gave reliability for both measures; the correction is an assumption. Recall bias may inflate questionnaire values.
agent_relevance: Chess is a highly predictable rule domain, so practice pays most there. Open-ended agent tasks are less predictable, so expect weaker returns.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) meta-analysis (starting age)
finding: Starting age predicts chess rating after practice is controlled, so an early start is not just extra hours.
numbers: Reports that Gobet & Campitelli (2007) and Howard (2012) both found earlier starting age predicted higher rating after controlling accumulated DP.
limits: Self-reported hours, so the control for DP is imperfect. Macnamara cites these studies; they are not tested again.
agent_relevance: Suggests a sensitive-period or learning-rate component. Exposure order may matter, not only total volume.

source: Gobet, Campitelli (2007) The role of domain-specific practice, handedness, and starting age in chess (secondary report in Hambrick 2020)
finding: Buenos Aires chess club sample: solitary plus group practice hours correlated moderately with rating, with a huge spread in hours needed for master.
numbers: N = 90 club members, r = 0.42 (about 18% variance). Hours to reach master ranged 3,016 to 23,608 (factor of nearly 8). Ericsson & Harwell cite 1,612 to 14,196 for solitary practice alone.
limits: Read only as reported by Hambrick 2020 and Ericsson & Harwell 2019, not the primary paper. Retrospective self-report.
agent_relevance: Two players with the same rating can have needed 8 times different practice. Budgeting compute by a fixed amount per level would misfire.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: is that all it takes to become an expert? (as summarised in Hambrick 2020)
finding: Reanalysis of 6 chess and 8 music studies: practice explains about a third of reliable variance.
numbers: Mean r = .49 chess, .43 music before correction. Assumed reliability .80 for DP. Reliable variance explained: 34% chess, 29.9% music. Chess rating reliability .91.
limits: Reliability .80 for DP is an assumption from Tuffiash et al. and Ericsson. Only 6 chess studies.
agent_relevance: Chess practice effect is mid-sized and robust but incomplete. Other factors, such as ability and starting age, carry about two-thirds.

source: Hambrick, Altmann, Oswald, Meinz, Gobet (2014) Facing facts about deliberate practice (reply to Platz et al.)
finding: Defends the variance framing. A correlation of 0.61 still leaves room for two other predictors of near 0.56 each.
numbers: Platz music rc = .61. Authors say r and r-squared are both valid indexes, that retrospective estimates could inflate r, and that Platz mixed in non-DP measures.
quote: deliberate practice is not as important as Ericsson and colleagues have argued
limits: Reply piece; no new data. Co-author Gobet is a chess researcher.
agent_relevance: Method lesson: an unfalsifiable defence (always blame the practice measure) should be avoided in our own agent evaluations.

source: Platz, Kopiez, Lehmann, Wolf (2014) The influence of deliberate practice on musical achievement: a meta-analysis
finding: Competing meta-analysis (music, not chess) reads similar data as a large effect and says Macnamara underestimates.
numbers: 13 studies, total N = 788, aggregated corrected correlation rc = 0.61, 95% CI [0.54, 0.67].
limits: Music only, small N, own inclusion criteria. Corrected for reliability. Hambrick says 0.61 could be an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Shows how analysis choices swing the verdict: 36% versus 21% of variance on overlapping literature.

source: Ericsson, Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Ericsson side: much of the skill gap is practice type. Solitary study in chess is DP-like but weaker than teacher-guided study; chess diaries match recall.
numbers: Chess diary study (de Bruin et al. 2008): weekly estimates correlated with diary values, r(34) = 0.6-0.8 range across chess and music. Glickman & Jones: chess rating reliability alpha .95 for masters, 0.59 for typical players. Practice-history variables explained over 50% of chess variance (Burgoyne 2019).
limits: Ericsson is the theory author. Excludes Howard (2012) as a single-number estimate. Argues Macnamara mixed practice types.
agent_relevance: Supports a typed-practice view: what kind of practice, not just how much. Same logic as scoring training episodes by type.

source: Charness, Tuffiash, Krampe, Reingold, Vasyukova (2005) The role of deliberate practice in chess expertise (as described in Hambrick 2020 and Ericsson & Harwell 2019)
finding: Main chess DP study: solitary serious study was the best predictor of rating; playing games added little once study was controlled.
numbers: Not read directly. Hambrick 2020 reports it found solitary study the best predictor and no reliable benefit from playing games after controlling it. Earlier chapter (1996) Study 1 N=136 of eventual 239.
limits: Retrospective self-report. Ericsson called it the most compelling chess evidence in 2005, then rejected it in 2014 for lacking a coach record.
agent_relevance: Anticipates the chess.com result: study beats play. In agent terms, analysis of positions beats more self-play games.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible? (inconsistency analysis)
finding: Documents that Ericsson's own classification of the Charness chess studies shifted between 2005 and 2014.
numbers: Ericsson (2014a) rejected Charness 2005 for no teacher record, but cited it positively in Ericsson (2014c). Ericsson & Harwell (2019) meta-analysis included 14 studies.
limits: Written by critics of Ericsson.
agent_relevance: A theory whose definition moves is hard to test. Our schema should fix what counts as a valid training episode up front (G3).

source: Burgoyne et al. (2016) The relationship between cognitive ability and chess skill: a comprehensive meta-analysis (via Hambrick 2020 and Ericsson & Harwell 2019)
finding: Cognitive ability matters more at lower chess skill. Ericsson predicts that fading; the data partly agree.
numbers: Fluid intelligence correlated significantly more strongly in lower-skill than higher-skill players (averages not captured). Not significant for highly skilled players per Ericsson & Harwell.
limits: Not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Raw ability helps early; domain knowledge dominates later. Scaffold gains may be larger for weaker base reasoners.

source: Burgoyne et al. (2019) practice-history variables explain over 50% of chess rating (via Ericsson & Harwell 2019)
finding: When many practice-history variables are modelled together, variance explained exceeds half.
numbers: Over 50% of variance in chess rating without correcting for attenuation.
limits: Second-hand; several correlated predictors; self-report.
agent_relevance: Upper bound: even rich practice data leave a large remainder.

source: Southwick, Harwell, Wright, Olsen, Ogles (2026) Not All Practice Is Created Equal: Longitudinal Evidence From Over 40,000 Chess Players (abstract only)
finding: Objective time-stamped chess.com data: practice-aligned activities (study) beat plain game play for rating gain.
numbers: N = 44,213 players. More than 90% of time spent on games. DP-aligned activities had 3.61x learning efficiency versus gameplay (ps < .001). Not all DP activities equal.
limits: Abstract only (full text behind paywall). Observational; selection into activities is not random. Author list includes an Ericsson-camp name (Harwell).
agent_relevance: Key chess evidence for this subfield. Targeted training on analysis and puzzles outperforms self-play volume per unit time.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess (ChessBench)
finding: Supervised training on Stockfish action values, with no search at test time, yields grandmaster-level play and scales with data and size.
numbers: 10M games, 15B data points. 270M transformer: Lichess blitz 2895 vs humans, 2299 vs bots, puzzle accuracy 95.4%. 136M: 94.5%; 9M: 88.9%. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct puzzle 66.5%. AlphaZero policy net 56.1%.
limits: Supervised distillation from an engine, not practice with feedback in the DP sense. The humans-vs-bots Elo gap shows style effects.
agent_relevance: Dense expert feedback (oracle labels) trains strong skill: an AI analogue of coached DP. Model size and data both matter.

source: McIlroy-Young, Sen, Kleinberg, Anderson (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system (Maia)
finding: Engines that play best do not predict human moves well. Maia, trained on human games per skill band, does.
numbers: Stockfish/Leela match human moves 33-41% (best 46%). Maia accuracy above 52% at best; lowest 46% when the 1900 model predicts 1100 players. Table: 50.8% (1100) to 52.9% (1900).
limits: Move-matching is not a learning curve. Lichess blitz data only.
agent_relevance: Person- and level-specific skill models exist. Useful for tutoring scaffolds, where practice must target the learner's level.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero
finding: A network learning from self-play alone acquires human chess concepts in a staged order during training.
numbers: Training of 1,000,000 steps. Many concepts start rising near 32,000 steps; piece values converge towards accepted values after 128,000 steps.
limits: Probing is correlational. Self-play is not human DP. Neural net, not a language model.
agent_relevance: Self-play practice yields knowledge in a predictable order. Curriculum sequencing could copy that order.

source: Schut et al. (2025) Bridging the human-AI knowledge gap through concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero (PNAS)
finding: Concepts mined from AlphaZero can be taught to top human grandmasters through puzzle-solution prototypes, and they improve.
numbers: Four grandmasters, 36-48 puzzles each, 13 concepts. Puzzles solved phase 1 to phase 3: GM1 0/12 to 5/12, GM2 4/12 to 7/12, GM3 3/12 to 5/12, GM4 6/16 to 7/15. Improved on 8 concepts, same on 3, worse on 2. Mean gain 0.85 puzzles, SE 0.12.
limits: Tiny N. Four participants, different concept sets. No control group. Short learning phase.
agent_relevance: A measured example of designed practice with feedback improving experts. Prototype pairs shown before the answer resemble worked-example operators.

source: Schut et al. (2025) PNAS (machine-student teaching test)
finding: Teaching an AI student from concept-specific prototypes beats teaching from random positions.
numbers: At the 16K-iteration AZ checkpoint, concept-specific training improved the student more than random sampling (Fig. 4). Novelty filter kept concepts whose AZ-basis reconstruction error beat the human-game basis across k (120 concepts in layer 19 examined).
limits: Figures only; exact student scores not read.
agent_relevance: Targeted examples beat random ones: a computational echo of practice type mattering.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) ChessLLM: Complete chess games enable LLM to become a chess master
finding: Plain supervised fine-tuning of an LLM on complete games gives professional level; data quality (long games) matters.
numbers: Elo 1788 vs standard Stockfish with 10 samples. Wins 61% at Stockfish skill 0, 56% at level 1, 30% at level 2. Long-round data gives +350 Elo over short-round. Over 20B tokens.
limits: Sampling 10 times is best-of-N. Opponent is weak Stockfish levels.
agent_relevance: Data quality beats raw amount; best-of-N sampling adds strength. Echoes DP quality over quantity.

source: Ericsson, Harwell (2019): reliability and range-restriction argument
finding: Ericsson argues low correlations arise from restricted range, since players need a rating before being measured.
numbers: Range-restriction correction estimates larger population correlations. Chess rating reliability alpha .95 masters, 0.59 for typical players (Glickman & Jones 1999).
limits: Corrections need the true range. Hambrick says they can be abused.
agent_relevance: Both sides agree measurement error matters. Report reliability for any agent-skill metric.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020): the DP definition problem
finding: Three claims blur: DP is any structured practice; DP is teacher-led practice; DP is practice that explains most variance.
numbers: Macnamara 2014 ended from over 11,000 articles screened; the 2014 reanalysis used 6 chess and 8 music studies.
limits: Position paper by critics.
agent_relevance: Name the practice type in each scaffold operator so claims remain testable.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020): circumvention-of-limits
finding: Ericsson predicts general ability stops mattering as skill grows. Chess is the strongest support, but one of 15 studies in a wider review.
numbers: Review of about 1,300 articles identified 15 studies; the chess meta-analysis (Burgoyne 2016) is the favourable one.
limits: Authors call evidence for the hypothesis weak and inconsistent in other complex tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not assume knowledge fully replaces reasoning strength.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014): publication bias check
finding: Funnel and trim-and-fill style checks found no missing effects, so the games effect is not a publication artifact.
numbers: Games 26% variance vs professions under 1% (p=.62) and education 4%. Moderator: by measure of performance, group membership r=.51, laboratory task r=.37, expert rating r=.30, standardized objective measure r=.28.
limits: Group membership (amateur vs pro) inflates r; chess rating counts as the stricter measure.
agent_relevance: Compare conditions with a continuous, objective score, not pass/fail group labels.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024): scaling behaviour
finding: Strength depends on both data set size and model size; small models fail even with supervision.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy 88.9% (9M), 94.5% (136M), 95.4% (270M). Only 1.33% of puzzle states appear in the training set.
limits: Puzzle accuracy saturates; blitz Elo vs bots only 2299.
agent_relevance: Practice volume helps only if capacity exists. No search at test time suggests knowledge can replace some computation.
